metadata.title: GASTROINTESTINAL SYSTEM (GIT) OSCE
metadata.subtitle: 15 Evidence-Corrected Stations
metadata.audienceAndScoring: Final-Year MBBS • 8 minutes per station • 20-point analytic checklist
metadata.facultyNote: This manual contains exactly 15 standalone final-year MBBS gastrointestinal-system OSCE stations, written for KMU- pattern final-year MBBS and postgraduate (CPSP) examinations. Stations 1–10 are clinically revised versions of the candidate's own supplied GIT teaching material (viral hepatitis, dyspepsia/peptic ulcer disease, irritable bowel syndrome, constipation, acute viral gastroenteritis, bacterial food poisoning, chronic diarrhoea, inflammatory bowel disease, neonatal jaundice) — patient names throughout have been changed from the source material. Stations 11– 15 broaden coverage across upper GI bleeding, acute pancreatitis, adult jaundice/abnormal liver blood tests, coeliac disease, and acute appendicitis. Local protocols supersede imported guidance. NICE, British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG), WHO/AASLD-IDSA, and WSES recommendations are used as identified evidence standards. They do not create Pakistani legal, licensing, prescribing, referral, or service obligations. Faculty must replace imported operational details with the current approved institutional, provincial, and national protocols before summative use. Resource constraints may shape implementation but must not reduce emergency safety.
assessmentDesign: Each station is designed for 8 minutes and uses a 20-point analytic checklist (10 observable items scored 0, 1, or 2).
Score 2 = clearly and independently achieved; 1 = partially achieved or achieved only after a standard prompt; 0 = omitted, incorrect, or unsafe.
The analytic score and global rating must be recorded independently. No numerical pass mark is prescribed; use an approved standard-setting process.
Critical safety errors require examiner review and may justify failure when they create material danger. A minor omission alone should not automatically fail a candidate.
Candidate learning notes are intended for release after the station unless faculty deliberately uses the page for formative open-book teaching.
Standardised prompts restore progress without revealing the answer. Record every prompt and apply the same scoring rule to every candidate.
printingAndAssembly: Each station begins on a new page. Candidate-facing material precedes a marked "Examiner confidential" break.
Remove or cover the Learning Note paragraph if the handout is used during a summative station.
Verify medicines, emergency charts, laboratory reference ranges, referral contacts, and equipment against the local site before use.

stations.title: Chronic Hepatitis B
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, serology interpretation, and counselling
candidateInstructions: Mr Waqas Ilyas, aged 34 years, attends after a routine blood donation screen returned a positive hepatitis B surface antigen.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, interpret the supplied serology panel, and counsel him on diagnosis, infectivity, transmission prevention, and follow-up.
Do not name a specific antiviral dose; discuss treatment at a class/pathway level.
candidateHandout: Serology: HBsAg positive, HBeAg positive (high infectivity), anti-HBc IgM negative (suggesting a picture more consistent with chronic than acute infection, to be confirmed on repeat testing at 6 months), liver function tests mildly elevated.
No current jaundice, no ascites, no encephalopathy; feels well; found only because of the blood-donation screen.
learningNotes: Learning note (release after the station): NICE CG165 (Hepatitis B: chronic diagnosis and management) supports confirming chronicity (HBsAg persisting beyond 6 months), assessing viral replication (HBeAg, HBV DNA) and liver damage (LFTs, fibrosis assessment), and referral to a specialist hepatology/infectious-disease service for consideration of antiviral therapy (e.g. a nucleos(t)ide analogue or pegylated interferon) when indicated. Sexual and household contacts need testing and vaccination if non-immune; safe-sex advice, avoidance of blood/razor/toothbrush sharing, and universal precautions are essential. All pregnancies in an affected woman need discussion of neonatal immunoprophylaxis to prevent vertical transmission.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I was told my blood donation test came back positive for hepatitis B. I feel completely fine."

If asked: no jaundice, no abdominal swelling, no confusion, no unintentional weight loss; no known IV drug use; had unprotected sex with more than one partner in the past; no tattoos; not vaccinated against hepatitis B; married, wife's status unknown.
ICE: worried about infecting his wife and future children; frightened this means his liver is already failing; wants to know if this is curable.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Full marks require the candidate to explain chronic infection versus a resolving acute infection, explicitly plan repeat testing to confirm chronicity, and correctly identify HBeAg positivity as marking high infectivity.
Expect referral for specialist assessment rather than a primary-care antiviral decision, and explicit advice about testing/vaccinating the wife and future children (neonatal immunoprophylaxis).
Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a history of risk factors (unprotected sex, needle-stick/tattoo exposure, family history), symptom screen (jaundice, weight loss, ascites, encephalopathy), and reproductive plans.

Interpret the serology: HBsAg-positive with HBeAg-positive indicates active viral replication and high infectivity; explain that chronicity is confirmed once HBsAg persists beyond 6 months, so repeat testing is needed.

Explain that hepatitis B is generally a manageable, sometimes suppressible but not always curable chronic infection; refer to hepatology/infectious disease for HBV DNA, fibrosis assessment, and consideration of antiviral therapy.
Advise safe sex, avoidance of sharing razors/toothbrushes, and testing and vaccination of household/sexual contacts, including his wife.
Discuss that future pregnancies need neonatal hepatitis B immunoprophylaxis (vaccine ± immunoglobulin) to prevent vertical transmission, and arrange follow-up.

Take a focused risk-factor and symptom history.
Interpret the serology in plain language.
Explain chronicity confirmation and the referral pathway.
Counsel on contact testing/vaccination and reproductive planning.
Arrange follow-up and check understanding.

Takes a focused risk-factor history (sexual, needle/tattoo exposure, family history).
Screens for symptoms of liver disease (jaundice, weight loss, ascites, encephalopathy).

stations.title: Hepatitis C
stations.primaryCompetency: Diagnosis explanation and antiviral cure counselling
candidateInstructions: Mr Rizwan Sadiq, aged 41 years, has tested anti-HCV positive after a pre-surgical screen, with HCV RNA confirming active infection.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain the diagnosis, and counsel on modern curative antiviral treatment and prevention of transmission.
Do not name a specific antiviral regimen duration/dose beyond "a curative all-oral tablet course"; refer detailed regimen selection to specialist care.
candidateHandout: History: had a blood transfusion years ago during a surgical procedure; no current jaundice, fatigue is mild; no known cirrhosis.
Investigations: anti-HCV positive, HCV RNA positive (confirms active/current infection, not just past exposure), liver function tests mildly elevated.
learningNotes: Learning note: Modern hepatitis C treatment uses short courses (typically around 8–12 weeks) of direct-acting antiviral tablets (e.g. sofosbuvir-based combinations), achieving cure (sustained virological response) in the great majority of patients, per WHO and AASLD-IDSA guidance. Unlike hepatitis B, hepatitis C is now considered curable in most cases with these regimens. Pre-treatment assessment includes degree of liver fibrosis/cirrhosis, genotype where locally relevant, and screening for other blood-borne infections. Prevention counselling covers safe injection practices, avoiding shared razors/needles, and blood-product screening; sexual transmission risk is low but not zero.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, they found hepatitis C in my blood before my operation. Is this something serious?"
If asked: transfusion during surgery many years ago; no IV drug use; mild tiredness only; no jaundice, no abdominal swelling; not aware of any other affected family member.
ICE: assumes hepatitis C is a lifelong incurable illness like he has heard about hepatitis B; worried about needing lifelong injections; worried about infecting his family.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Full marks require the candidate to correctly and clearly state that modern treatment is curative in most patients (distinguishing this from the chronic-suppression model of hepatitis B) and to describe treatment at the class level (short oral antiviral course) without needing to specify an exact regimen.
Expect referral for genotype/fibrosis assessment and treatment initiation by a specialist service, plus advice on preventing transmission to others. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a history of exposure risk (transfusion, IV drug use, tattoos, needle-stick), symptoms of liver disease, and family/contact risk.
Explain that HCV RNA positivity confirms active current infection, distinct from anti-HCV alone (which can reflect past exposure).

Correct the patient's assumption: explain that, unlike hepatitis B, most hepatitis C infection is now curable with a short course of modern oral antiviral tablets, with cure confirmed by an undetectable HCV RNA some weeks after finishing treatment.
Refer to a specialist hepatology/infectious-disease service for fibrosis assessment, genotype testing where relevant, and treatment initiation.
Counsel on preventing transmission (no sharing razors/needles, safe injection practices if relevant, low but non-zero sexual transmission risk) and arrange follow-up.
suggestedApproach: Explore the patient's understanding and correct any false assumption about incurability.
Take a focused exposure and symptom history.
Explain the diagnosis and the curative treatment pathway.
Refer for specialist fibrosis/genotype assessment and treatment.
Counsel on transmission prevention.
Arrange follow-up and check understanding.

checklist.criterion: Explores the patient's existing understanding and corrects the "incurable" assumption.
Takes a focused history of exposure risk (transfusion, IV drug use, tattoos).
Screens for symptoms/signs of chronic liver disease.
Correctly explains the difference between anti-HCV and HCV RNA positivity.

Explains how cure is confirmed (undetectable HCV RNA after treatment).

stations.title: Dyspepsia, GORD & Peptic Ulcer Disease
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, differential diagnosis, and stepwise management
candidateInstructions: Mr Sarmad Yousaf presents with epigastric pain and burning behind the chest, with bloating, wind, nausea, and occasional vomiting.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, screen for red flags, and outline a stepwise lifestyle-then-drug management plan.
Do not perform endoscopy yourself; describe when it would be arranged.
candidateHandout: Symptoms for several weeks: epigastric burning, worse with certain foods, bloating, wind, nausea, occasional vomiting; no reported weight loss, no black stools, no persistent vomiting, no palpable mass.
Personal history: smoker, drinks alcohol regularly, fond of coffee/chocolate/spicy food; takes occasional over-the-counter ibuprofen for headaches.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE CG184 (Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults) supports lifestyle advice (weight loss, smaller meals, avoiding late meals, raising the head of the bed, reducing trigger foods/alcohol/smoking) as first-line, then a full-dose proton pump inhibitor trial (e.g. omeprazole) for 4 weeks. Test-and-treat for Helicobacter pylori (urea breath test or stool antigen; avoid endoscopy purely to test) is offered if the PPI trial fails or before starting the PPI, followed by eradication therapy (a PPI plus two antibiotics) if positive. Red flags (dysphagia, weight loss, persistent vomiting, GI bleeding, epigastric mass, age with new onset) mandate urgent referral for endoscopy rather than continued empirical treatment.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I've had this burning pain behind my chest and in my stomach area, with a lot of bloating and wind."

If asked: pain is worse after spicy/fatty food and coffee; sometimes feels food/acid coming back into his mouth; no difficulty swallowing; no black stools; no unintentional weight loss; takes occasional ibuprofen for headaches.
If asked about timing: pain both soon after eating and sometimes a couple of hours later (candidate should ask, not assume, and reason about gastric vs duodenal pattern where relevant).
ICE: worried he might have stomach cancer because a friend was recently diagnosed; wants a quick fix, ideally without long-term tablets.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Full marks require explicit red-flag screening (dysphagia, weight loss, GI bleeding, persistent vomiting, epigastric mass) before reassuring, and identification of NSAID use as a relevant contributing drug.
Accept lifestyle advice plus a PPI trial as the correct first step, with H. pylori test-and-treat and endoscopy reserved appropriately as above. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a history of the pain's timing, character, relation to food and posture, and associated symptoms (bloating, wind, nausea, vomiting, reflux sensation).

Explicitly screen red flags: dysphagia, unintentional weight loss, persistent vomiting, evidence of GI bleeding (black stool), epigastric mass — any of these warrants urgent referral for endoscopy rather than empirical treatment.
Review personal and drug history: smoking, alcohol, caffeine, trigger foods, and NSAID/other ulcerogenic drug use, addressing NSAID use directly.
Advise lifestyle measures (diet, weight, reducing trigger foods/alcohol/smoking, raising the head of the bed, earlier evening meals) as first-line, then a 4-week full-dose PPI trial.

If symptoms persist: test for H. pylori (breath/stool test) and treat with eradication therapy if positive; if the picture still does not resolve, or red flags emerge, refer for endoscopy; also refer routinely if the patient remains anxious about cancer or needs ongoing NSAID treatment.
suggestedApproach: Take a structured pain and symptom history.
Screen red flags explicitly before reassuring.
Review lifestyle and drug contributors, including NSAID use.
Advise lifestyle measures first.
Offer a PPI trial, then H. pylori test-and-treat if needed.
Explain when endoscopy would be arranged and safety-net.

checklist.criterion: Takes a structured history of pain character, timing, and relation to food/posture.
Explores associated symptoms: bloating, wind, nausea, vomiting, reflux sensation.
Explicitly screens red flags (dysphagia, weight loss, bleeding, persistent vomiting, mass).
Reviews smoking, alcohol, caffeine, and dietary triggers.

stations.title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, positive diagnosis, and holistic counselling
candidateInstructions: Ms Rabia Hameed, aged 24 years, has had abdominal pain and altered bowel habit for 5 years. Prior investigations have all been normal.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history using a positive-diagnosis approach, screen red flags and differentials, and counsel on a stepwise management plan.
Do not order repeat extensive investigation without justification; explain IBS as a positive diagnosis, not one of exclusion alone.
candidateHandout: Symptoms for 5 years: abdominal pain relieved by defecation, bloating/distension, altered bowel habit (looser stools with urgency-free straining pattern), sensation of incomplete evacuation, passage of mucus, symptoms worse after eating.
No blood in stool, no nocturnal diarrhoea, no fever, no unintentional weight loss; family history of an anxious mother; periods are heavy and painful (relevant differential).
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE CG61 (Irritable bowel syndrome in adults) supports a positive diagnosis based on abdominal pain/discomfort with at least two of: relief with defecation, altered stool frequency, or altered stool form, plus at least two of: altered stool passage, bloating, worse after eating, or mucus passage — once red flags are excluded. First-line investigations (in patients under about 40 without red flags) are limited to FBC, ESR/CRP, and coeliac serology. Management combines dietary/lifestyle advice, first-line antispasmodics or laxatives/antimotility agents matched to the predominant symptom, and low-dose tricyclic antidepressants as a second-line option for pain, with psychological therapies reserved for refractory cases.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I've had stomach pain and irregular bowel movements for years. All my tests have come back normal."
If asked: pain improves after opening bowels; bloating is prominent; no blood in stool; no weight loss; no night-time diarrhoea; periods are heavy and painful; mother was "always an anxious person."
Differential screening: no worsening with wheat specifically beyond general dietary sensitivity; no vaginal discharge or pain during intercourse; no particular heat/cold intolerance.
ICE: frustrated at being told "it's just stress"; worried there's a missed diagnosis; wants to know if this will ever go away.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Full marks require the candidate to build a positive diagnosis (pain + defecation-related pattern + at least two supporting features) rather than simply excluding disease, while still screening the relevant red flags and gynaecological/thyroid differentials.
Accept FBC/ESR-CRP/coeliac serology as sufficient first-line testing for a patient under 40 without red flags; do not reward ordering colonoscopy routinely at this age/presentation.
Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a history using the ABC framework (abdominal pain, bloating, change in bowel habit) plus the supporting features (incomplete evacuation, mucus, worse after eating) to build a positive diagnosis.

Screen red flags (blood in stool, weight loss, fever, nocturnal diarrhoea, new onset over 40 with a change in bowel habit, family history of bowel/ovarian cancer) and relevant differentials (coeliac disease, gynaecological disease, thyroid disease).

Explain that first-line testing (FBC, ESR/CRP, coeliac serology ± further tests if over 40 or red flags present) is enough given the reassuring history, and that IBS is a positive diagnosis, not one reached only by exclusion.

Counsel on diet/lifestyle (regular meals, adequate fluid, tailored fibre, stress management), and offer first-line drug therapy matched to symptom pattern (antispasmodic for pain, a laxative if constipation-predominant, an antimotility agent if diarrhoea-predominant), with low-dose tricyclic as a second-line pain option.
Validate the patient's frustration, avoid dismissive language, and safety-net for the return of any red-flag feature; offer referral if diagnosis remains in doubt or treatment fails.
suggestedApproach: Take an ABC-structured history to build a positive diagnosis.
Screen red flags and relevant differentials.
Explain the diagnosis in validating, non-dismissive language.
Justify limited first-line investigation.
Offer stepwise diet/lifestyle and drug management matched to symptom pattern.

stations.title: Chronic Constipation
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused assessment, red-flag screening, and stepwise laxative management
candidateInstructions: Mr Iftikhar Zaman, aged 52 years, reports passing hard, infrequent stools with straining for the past several months.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, screen for organic/red-flag causes appropriate to his age, and outline a stepwise management plan.
Do not skip rectal examination in your description; verbalise it as part of your assessment plan.
candidateHandout: Symptoms: fewer than 2 bowel movements per week, hard/lumpy stool, straining, sensation of incomplete evacuation, for more than 3 months.

No blood in stool, no unintentional weight loss, no nocturnal diarrhoea, no family history of bowel cancer; takes a calcium-channel blocker (verapamil) for blood pressure, which the candidate should recognise as a possible contributor.
learningNotes: Learning note: In a patient over 40 with a new, sustained change in bowel habit, red flags (blood in stool, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal/rectal mass, family history of colorectal cancer) must be actively excluded, and abdominal plus rectal examination is part of the assessment (to check for faecal impaction and exclude a low rectal mass). Reversible contributors (rate-limiting calcium-channel blockers such as verapamil/diltiazem, opioids, iron, anticholinergics, hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia) should be reviewed. Management is stepwise: lifestyle (fluid, fibre, activity) first, then an osmotic laxative (e.g. a macrogol), adding or switching to a stimulant laxative (e.g. senna) if needed, with rectal measures (suppositories) or an enema considered for refractory impaction.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, I've been terribly constipated for months now — I strain a lot and don't feel properly empty afterwards."
If asked: no blood in stool, no weight loss, no family history of bowel problems; drinks little water during the workday; sedentary desk job; takes verapamil for blood pressure.
If asked for examination: state abdomen soft and non-tender with no palpable mass; rectal examination (if requested) shows hard stool in the rectum, no mass, normal tone.
ICE: worried this might be cancer because a colleague was recently diagnosed with bowel cancer; wants "a strong medicine to sort it out quickly."
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Full marks require explicit red-flag screening given his age (over 40 with a new symptom), identification of verapamil as a reversible contributor, and verbalising abdominal and rectal examination.

Accept a stepwise osmotic-then-stimulant laxative plan; do not reward jumping straight to an enema or a stimulant laxative as first-line without trying lifestyle/osmotic measures first, unless faecal impaction is described.
Prompted items score at most 1/2.
keyAnswerGuide: Take a history confirming the constipation definition (frequency, consistency, straining, incomplete evacuation) and its duration.
Actively screen red flags given his age (blood in stool, weight loss, family history, anaemia symptoms) — any positive finding warrants further investigation/referral.
Review medicines and identify verapamil as a possible contributor, alongside other causes (hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, low fluid/fibre intake, immobility).
Verbalise abdominal examination for masses/hepatomegaly and rectal examination to exclude impaction or a low rectal mass.

Manage stepwise: lifestyle advice (fluid, fibre, activity) first; if insufficient, an osmotic laxative; add or switch to a stimulant laxative if still inadequate; consider rectal measures for impaction; review/adjust the contributing medicine where clinically appropriate rather than stopping it unilaterally.

Screen red flags given his age.
Review medicines and other reversible causes.
Examine abdomen and rectum (verbalised).
Give stepwise lifestyle-then-laxative management.
Address his cancer concern honestly and arrange follow-up.

Explicitly screens red flags appropriate to age over 40 with a new symptom.
Reviews medicines and identifies verapamil as a possible contributor.
Screens other reversible causes (thyroid, calcium, fluid/fibre intake, immobility).
Verbalises abdominal examination for masses/organomegaly.

stations.title: Acute Viral Gastroenteritis
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, dehydration assessment, and supportive management
candidateInstructions: Mr Kashif Rauf, visiting from abroad, presents with 2 days of watery diarrhoea, vomiting, and generalised weakness.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, assess for dehydration, and outline supportive management, safety-netting, and occupational advice (he works as a chef).
Do not prescribe an antibiotic; explain why one is not indicated here.
candidateHandout: Symptoms for 2 days: watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea, 3–4 stools/day, vomiting, generalised weakness; no blood or mucus in stool; a household contact has similar symptoms.
No fever documented; mild signs of dehydration (dry mouth, thirst) but alert and able to drink.
learningNotes: Learning note: Most acute watery diarrhoea with vomiting in a well-looking adult is viral gastroenteritis and is self-limiting; management is supportive — oral rehydration solution, gradual reintroduction of bland food, avoiding antimotility agents if fever/bloody stool is present, and antiemetics/antispasmodics for symptom relief as needed. candidateInstructions: Mrs Samina Toqeer, aged 48 years, developed diarrhoea, vomiting, and weakness a few hours after eating barbecued meat at a restaurant.

candidateHandout: Onset 1–6 hours after eating barbecued meat, with several other family members who ate the same meal similarly affected — a pattern consistent with a preformed bacterial toxin (e.g. Staphylococcus aureus) rather than an invasive bacterial infection.

learningNotes: Learning note: Toxin-mediated food poisoning (short incubation of 1–6 hours, clustering among people who shared the same meal, watery non-bloody diarrhoea) is typically self-limiting over 24–48 hours and does not require antibiotics, because the illness is caused by preformed toxin rather than ongoing bacterial invasion — antibiotics do not shorten it and are not routinely indicated. Management is rehydration (oral rehydration solution, or IV fluids and hospital admission if there is significant dehydration/high stool frequency such as this patient's), antiemetic/antispasmodic symptom relief, and safety-netting. Antibiotics are reserved for specific invasive bacterial diarrhoeal illness with systemic features, immunocompromise, or specific stool-culture-identified pathogens where guidelines support treatment (e.g. severe Campylobacter, invasive Shigella) — not given empirically for a classic short-incubation toxin-mediated picture.

candidateInstructions: Mr Adeel Farooq, aged 38 years, reports loose stools for the past 3 months, more frequent than his usual pattern.

stations.title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (Ulcerative Colitis vs Crohn's Disease)
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history and differential diagnosis between the two major inflammatory bowel diseases
candidateInstructions: Ms Kiran Abbasi, aged 27 years, presents with several weeks of bloody diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and weight loss.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history and examination-oriented assessment to differentiate ulcerative colitis from Crohn's disease, and outline the initial investigation and referral plan.

candidateHandout: Symptoms: bloody, mucoid diarrhoea for several weeks, lower abdominal cramping pain, low-grade fever, tiredness, and unintentional weight loss; no mouth ulcers, no perianal symptoms volunteered (ask directly).

learningNotes: Learning note: Ulcerative colitis more typically presents with continuous, blood/mucus-predominant diarrhoea confined to colonic mucosa, is more common in non-smokers (smoking appears protective), and is associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis and continuous relapse in the same bowel segment. Crohn's disease more typically presents with abdominal pain/cramping (transmural, skip lesions anywhere from mouth to anus), is a risk-increasing habit in smokers, and is associated with perianal fistulae/abscesses, mouth ulcers, malabsorption, and stricture/bowel obstruction. Both share extra-intestinal features (arthritis, uveitis/iritis, erythema nodosum) and constitutional symptoms. Initial work-up includes FBC, inflammatory markers, stool calprotectin and culture (to exclude infection), followed by colonoscopy with biopsy for definitive diagnosis; management follows NICE NG130 (ulcerative colitis) and NG129 (Crohn's disease) once confirmed.

stations.title: Neonatal Jaundice

candidateInstructions: Mrs Naseem Akhtar, aged 55 years, attends to discuss her 6-day-old grandson, who developed yellow discoloration of the skin and eyes from day 3 of life.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, interpret the supplied bilirubin trend, and counsel on management and safety-netting.

candidateHandout: Baby born at term, uneventful pregnancy and normal vaginal delivery; jaundice first noticed on day 3 of life (not within the first 24 hours); currently day 6.

learningNotes: Learning note: NICE CG98 (Jaundice in newborn babies under 28 days) treats jaundice appearing within the first 24 hours of life as always pathological, requiring urgent same-day paediatric assessment (for causes such as haemolysis or infection). Any jaundice at any time associated with an unwell baby, pale stools, or dark urine needs prompt paediatric referral, as does jaundice persisting beyond 14 days (21 in preterm infants).

stations.title: Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition, risk stratification, and protocol-based initial management
candidateInstructions: Mr Bilal Sarwar, aged 54 years, is brought in vomiting blood and passing black tarry stool.
In 8 minutes: lead immediate assessment and management, verbalising all orders to the nurse/examiner.
Do not delay resuscitation to complete a full history.
candidateHandout: A–E: airway patent; breathing normal rate; circulation shows tachycardia and borderline-low blood pressure; patient pale, clammy, and anxious but conscious and orientated.
History available on request: known heavy alcohol use; takes regular over-the-counter ibuprofen for back pain; one episode of fresh haematemesis and one episode of melaena so far.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE CG141 (Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding) supports immediate A–E resuscitation with IV access (two large-bore cannulae), crystalloid fluid resuscitation, and group-and-save/crossmatch, using a validated risk score (e.g. Glasgow-Blatchford at first assessment) to guide urgency, with restrictive red-cell transfusion (generally a threshold-based approach rather than reflexive transfusion) unless the patient is in shock or has ongoing major bleeding. Endoscopy is arranged urgently (within 24 hours, immediately if unstable) after resuscitation, and IV proton pump inhibitor therapy and correction of coagulopathy are considered per local protocol. A history of alcohol use and NSAID use both raise suspicion for variceal and peptic ulcer causes respectively, which changes pre-endoscopy management (e.g. terlipressin/antibiotics if variceal bleeding is suspected).

After IV access, fluids, and bloods (including crossmatch) are ordered: state a further small haematemesis occurs; blood pressure remains borderline.

If the candidate asks about suspected cause: state stigmata of chronic liver disease are present on brief examination if requested (e.g. mild scleral icterus), which should raise possible variceal bleeding as well as peptic ulcer disease given the NSAID history.

stations.title: Acute Pancreatitis
stations.primaryCompetency: Emergency recognition, diagnostic reasoning, and protocol-based initial management
candidateInstructions: Mr Yasir Chaudhry, aged 45 years, presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, with vomiting, after a heavy meal and alcohol the night before.
In 8 minutes: lead assessment, interpret the supplied investigation findings, and outline initial emergency management.
Do not wait for imaging before starting resuscitation.
candidateHandout: A–E: airway patent; breathing mildly increased rate; circulation shows tachycardia and borderline blood pressure; patient in obvious pain, unable to lie still, vomiting.

Investigation available on request: serum amylase/lipase significantly elevated (more than three times the upper limit of normal), consistent with acute pancreatitis; history of gallstones is unknown (ask directly) and alcohol intake is heavy.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE NG104 (Pancreatitis) supports diagnosis from two of three features (typical pain, amylase/lipase more than three times the upper limit of normal, or characteristic imaging findings) — a definite biochemical diagnosis here does not require imaging to confirm the diagnosis itself, though imaging (ultrasound for gallstones, contrast CT later if severity assessment or complications are in question) is still used to establish the cause and assess severity/complications. Initial management is aggressive IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, antiemetics, oxygen if hypoxic, monitoring for organ dysfunction, and early nutrition (oral/enteral as tolerated rather than routine prolonged fasting) once stabilising; severity scoring (e.g. Glasgow-Imrie criteria) guides the need for HDU/ICU care. Gallstones and alcohol are the two leading causes and should both be actively assessed for, since gallstone pancreatitis may need early ERCP/cholecystectomy planning.

After amylase/lipase result is requested: give the elevated result as per handout.

If the candidate delays treatment to await imaging: condition/pain worsens; provide the emergency stall prompt.

stations.title: Adult Jaundice / Abnormal Liver Blood Tests
stations.primaryCompetency: Data interpretation and structured referral planning
candidateInstructions: Mrs Farah Naveed, aged 46 years, attends with yellowing of the eyes and dark urine for one week; blood tests have been done.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, interpret the supplied liver blood test pattern, and outline the referral/investigation pathway.
Do not commit to a single cause without reasoning from the pattern of results supplied.
candidateHandout: Results: bilirubin raised; alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT disproportionately raised compared with ALT/AST (a cholestatic/obstructive pattern rather than a hepatocellular one).
History: pale stool and dark urine reported; itching present; mild right-upper-quadrant discomfort; no fever; no known alcohol excess; no new medicines started recently (ask directly).
learningNotes: Learning note: The British Society of Gastroenterology guideline on abnormal liver blood tests supports classifying the pattern as hepatocellular (ALT/AST disproportionately raised) versus cholestatic (ALP/GGT disproportionately raised) as the first step, since this determines the imaging and referral pathway. A cholestatic pattern with pale stool, dark urine, itching, and right-upper-quadrant discomfort raises suspicion of biliary obstruction (e.g. gallstone in the common bile duct, or a pancreatic/biliary mass in an older patient) and warrants urgent abdominal ultrasound, with MRCP/ERCP and hepatobiliary referral depending on findings. New-onset painless jaundice in an older adult, or jaundice with weight loss, needs urgent cancer-pathway referral to exclude a pancreaticobiliary malignancy.

stations.title: Coeliac Disease
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, correct investigation sequencing, and dietary counselling
candidateInstructions: Ms Amna Riasat, aged 29 years, presents with bloating, loose stools, tiredness, and unexplained low iron levels found on a recent blood test.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, explain correct serological testing, and counsel on management if coeliac disease is confirmed.
Do not advise her to start a gluten-free diet before testing is complete — this is a common and important error.
candidateHandout: Symptoms: bloating, loose stools, tiredness, and unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia on recent bloods; mild weight loss; no blood in stool; family history of a sibling with a similar bowel problem.
Currently eating a normal, gluten-containing diet.
learningNotes: Learning note: NICE NG20 (Coeliac disease: recognition, assessment and management) supports first-line serological testing with IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody (with total IgA to exclude IgA deficiency, which can cause a false-negative result), while the patient continues eating gluten-containing food for the duration of testing — stopping gluten before testing can cause a false-negative result and is a common, important error to avoid. A positive serology is followed by endoscopic duodenal biopsy to confirm the diagnosis. Once confirmed, management is a lifelong strict gluten-free diet with dietitian input, monitoring of nutritional status (iron, calcium, vitamin D, B12/folate), bone health assessment, and pneumococcal vaccination (due to hyposplenism risk) per local protocol.

stations.title: Acute Appendicitis
stations.primaryCompetency: Focused history, focused abdominal examination, and safe surgical referral
candidateInstructions: Mr Danish Iqbal, aged 22 years, presents with abdominal pain that started around the umbilicus and has moved to the right lower quadrant over the past day.
In 8 minutes: take a focused history, describe a focused abdominal examination, interpret the supplied findings, and outline the management/referral plan.
Do not delay surgical referral to complete extensive additional investigation in a classic presentation.
candidateHandout: History: pain started peri-umbilically and migrated to the right iliac fossa over 24 hours; associated with nausea, one episode of vomiting, low-grade fever, and reduced appetite; pain worse on movement/coughing.

Examination on request: low-grade fever, tenderness and guarding at McBurney's point, rebound tenderness present, positive cough/hop test (pain on coughing or hopping), Rovsing's sign positive (pain in the right iliac fossa on palpating the left); no palpable mass; no signs of generalised peritonitis (diffuse rigidity) at this point.
learningNotes: Learning note: The WSES (World Society of Emergency Surgery) 2020 Jerusalem guidelines support diagnosing acute appendicitis primarily on the clinical picture (migratory periumbilical-to-right-iliac-fossa pain, anorexia, low-grade fever, localised right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding/rebound) supported by inflammatory markers and, where diagnostic doubt remains (e.g. in women of reproductive age or atypical presentations), ultrasound or CT imaging. Management of confirmed or high-probability appendicitis is prompt surgical referral for appendicectomy (open or laparoscopic per local practice) with pre-operative analgesia, IV fluids, and antibiotics per local protocol; a clearly perforated/peritonitic presentation needs more urgent resuscitation and escalation. Non-operative antibiotic-only management is an evolving option in selected uncomplicated cases per some protocols, but remains a specialist surgical decision, not a primary-care one.
simulationScript: Opening: "Doctor, my stomach pain started around my belly button yesterday, and now it's moved to my right side and it's much worse."

If asked for examination: as per handout — tenderness/guarding at McBurney's point, rebound tenderness, positive cough/hop test, positive Rovsing's sign, no mass, no diffuse rigidity.
ICE: worried about needing "a big operation" and asks if it will definitely need surgery or if tablets could be tried instead.
examinerInstructions: Give the handout at the start. Provide examination findings only on request, and confirm findings as listed if the correct examination manoeuvre is performed/described.

Full marks require the candidate to recognise the classic migratory pain pattern, correctly interpret the examination findings as supporting appendicitis, and arrange prompt surgical referral with appropriate pre-referral supportive measures (analgesia, IV fluids, keeping the patient nil by mouth in anticipation of possible surgery).

Accept a brief, honest answer to the "tablets instead of surgery" question that correctly frames antibiotic-only management as a specialist/selected-case decision, not a routine alternative offered from primary care. Prompted items score at most 1/2.
